Today

Four things, one hour

  1. LinkedIn.Set it up once, then add to it slowly.
  2. Your resume.Print your profile, then cut it to one page.
  3. Build an app.Ten minutes in Google AI Studio.
  4. Show someone.That part is the networking.

Thirty seconds. The four tiles are the whole hour, in order.

Most people open LinkedIn the night before the career fair.

The scramble

Write everything at once, under pressure, and forget half of what you’ve done.

Set it up once

Build it tonight. Then add one line whenever something happens: a class project, a club role, a hackathon.

Sam’s framing: LinkedIn is a set-it-and-forget-it record that grows slowly. Press once for the right side.

Why bother

Everything worth pitching about you, in one place.

Every interview answer and every networking conversation pulls from the same list.

This is the point of the whole LinkedIn half: the profile is the list you pull from when someone says “tell me about yourself.”

Set it up once

The sections that matter

  1. Photo and headline.A photo gets up to 2x more profile views.
  2. About.Two or three lines, in your own voice.
  3. Experience and education.Jobs, clubs, research, tutoring. It all counts.
  4. Skills and projects.What you built, and what you built it with.

Each press moves the spotlight to the next section. Source for the photo stat: LinkedIn Help, “members with a profile photo receive up to 2X more profile views and 3X more connection requests” (linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a545557). Don’t quote the old 21x figure; it’s from a 2016 blog post. The diagram is ours, drawn from Sam’s resume, not a LinkedIn screenshot.

Then print it

Your profile, saved as a PDF, is resume draft one.

  1. Me, then View profile.
  2. More or Resources, then Save to PDF.On a laptop. The app can’t do it.
  3. Cut it to one page.That’s your resume, version one.

Path from LinkedIn Help (a541960): Me > View profile > More or Resources > Save to PDF. Desktop only, English profiles only, 200 PDFs a month. It briefly disappeared for some accounts in July 2025, so try it on your own profile before the meeting. The LinkedIn PDF runs long; the resume is the one-page edit of it.

Your turn · 8 minutes

Make an account. Then trade profiles.

8:00

No account? Make one now. Have one? Connect with two people you don’t know yet. In the app, tap the QR code in the search bar. T to start.

Eight minutes. People with accounts: introduce yourselves and connect in person. The app’s QR code (search bar > QR icon > My code / Scan) is from an older Help article (a525286); check where the icon is on your phone before the meeting. LinkedIn’s minimum age is 16.

How it works

How to connect without being weird

  1. Add a note.One line: where you met, or why you’re reaching out. Free accounts get 3 notes a month.
  2. Don’t pitch first.Ask a question. Nobody wants a sales pitch from a stranger.
  3. Reply and thank.A thank-you after a chat or an intro is what people remember.
  4. Keep it professional.It’s the one feed your future boss also reads.

Note limit from LinkedIn Help (a563153): up to three personalized invitations a month on a free account, 200 characters each. Blogs still say five; the live page says three.

Same request, two notes.

Ignored

“I’d like to add you to my professional network.”

Accepted

“Hi Maya, we met at the GDG meeting at RCC today. Loved your flashcard app. Let’s stay in touch!”

Maya is an example, not a real member. The second note is under 200 characters: where you met, one specific thing, and a light ask.

Why LinkedIn

It’s where the professional world actually is.

Jobs, people, and what’s changing, all in one feed.

Three features next: trends, jobs, and people.

Why LinkedIn

1.3 billion members.

And every minute, about 8,200 job applications and 18,000 new connections.

Source: news.linkedin.com/about-us, captured 2026-09-29: “~8.2K job applications are submitted” and “18K+ connections are made” every minute; “+1.3B members”. About page: members in more than 200 countries and territories. Presses: applications, connections, members.

Trends

See what’s growing before everyone else does.

LinkedIn’s 2026 list of the fastest-growing US jobs starts with AI engineers, then AI consultants and strategists.

Source: LinkedIn News, Jobs on the Rise 2026 (US), published Jan 7, 2026. Top three: AI engineers, AI consultants and strategists, new home sales specialists. Presses: the skills people have, where the jobs are, how much experience and where people came from, how much is remote. Skills on the Rise 2026 and Top Companies 2026 are on LinkedIn News too.

Jobs

Apply the day it’s posted.

A job alert tells you when one goes up. Easy Apply lets you apply without leaving LinkedIn.

A real search captured 2026-09-29. Presses: six days old, over 200 applicants; three hours old, “Be an early applicant”; the alert toggle; the Easy Apply filter. The “early applicant” label is on the real listing, but LinkedIn publishes no stat about early applicants, so don’t quote one. Alerts come daily or weekly by email or notification (Help a511279).

People

Your network is bigger than your contacts.

  1. 1st: people you know.Message them anytime.
  2. 2nd: people they know.Connect with a note, or ask for an intro.
  3. 3rd: one step further.Get closer through someone in between.

Definitions from LinkedIn Help (a545636): 1st are direct connections; 2nd are connected to your 1st; 3rd are connected to your 2nd. Messaging people outside your network is InMail, a Premium feature. The counts in the diagram are illustrative.

Start here

44000RCC alumni

are on LinkedIn. Look up where they work. Some of them work where you want to.

Source: linkedin.com/school/riverside-city-college/people, 2026-09-29: “What 44,624 Riverside City College alumni on LinkedIn are up to”, broken down by where they work, what they do, and what they studied. The page has about 50K followers. Say “about 44,000”; it changes daily.

Now the resume

LinkedIn is the archive. The resume is the pitch.

Same material, different job.

What matters on each

LinkedIn

Everything, always growing: your photo, your story, your whole history.

Resume

One page, for one job. Skimmed in 7 to 15 seconds, then read for 30 to 60 if it survives.

Scan times from Sam’s resume guide: TheLadders’ 2018 eye-tracking update put the first scan at 7.4 seconds; plan for 7 to 15 on the first pass and 30 to 60 for a resume that survives. One page for students: CMU SCS, Harvard FAS, Gayle Laakmann McDowell.

Real example

My resume, one page.

  1. The top third does the most work.Put your strongest proof there.
  2. Lead with what changed.Faster, bigger, first place.
  3. Numbers you can defend.If you can’t explain it out loud, cut it.
  4. Education last, for me.Proof first when you have it.

Sam’s own resume (career repo, built 2026-09-29) with the phone, email, and city removed for the public deck. Rules from his resume guide: one page, top third does the most work, cut any number you wouldn’t defend out loud.

What we were told to write

A trait

“Hard-working.”

Better: a real role

Peer tutor and TA for the CS data structures and algorithms sequence.

“Detail-oriented.”

Research intern analyzing ICPC programming-contest results.

“A natural leader.”

President of the GDG and ACM chapters at RCC.

Three presses, one row each. The right side is better because it names a real role. It still says nothing about how much or what changed; that’s next.

Better says what you did. Best says what changed.

Strong verb Impact

Better

Software engineering intern working on Redis caching.

Best: impact first

Cut load times up to ~55% by putting Redis caching in front of slow reads.

Built a robot at a hackathon.

Won 1st Place Overall at Citrus Hack 2026 with a robot that spots distress in dementia patients.

Peer tutor and TA for the CS data structures and algorithms sequence.

Run ~20 hours a week of tutoring for 150+ CS students.

All three bests are Sam’s real resume bullets, lightly shortened. Point at the order: the result comes before the how. Verbs from MIT CAPD’s list; banned: worked on, helped with, responsible for, leveraged.

The formula

Accomplished X, measured by Y, by doing Z.

Laszlo Bock, Google’s former head of People Operations.

Bock’s XYZ formula (2014). Example he gives: “Increased sales by 25% by launching a new line of business in Q1.” Yale, Princeton, Stanford, and MIT teach the same shape under other names.

Watch it change

Same you, three times.

  1. I’m hard-working and dependable.
  2. I tutor CS students in data structures and algorithms.
  3. I tutor 150+ CS students about 20 hours a week in data structures and algorithms.

Press twice. The last version is something you’d actually say out loud in an interview, which is the test.

One rule

If you have to say it, you haven’t shown it.

Cut: hard-working, passionate, detail-oriented, team player, responsible for, helped with.

From Sam’s bullet-pattern notes: every adjective you use about yourself gets cut and replaced with a behavior and a result.

Ten minutes

Now build something.

A small tool for one of your classes, made with AI in Google AI Studio.

No coding experience needed. Build mode (aistudio.google.com/apps) turns a description into a working app with a live preview.

Your prompt

Try this

  1. 1. Open aistudio.google.com, then Build.
  2. 2. “Build me a study tool for [class].”
  3. 3. Run it. Change one thing by chatting.

18+ with a personal Gmail. School accounts can’t use it under 18. Otherwise, pair up.

Facts: AI Studio requires age 18+ (Gemini API terms); Workspace for Education accounts under 18 are blocked; a personal Gmail is safest. Free tier: Google may review what you type, so no personal info in prompts. Sharing an app by link is free; public deploy is free for 2 apps on eligible personal accounts only. Have Sam’s own laptop ready as a backup demo if someone gets throttled.

Pairs · 2 minutes each

Show it to someone you don’t know.

4:00

What it does, why you made it, one thing you’d add next. Switch at 2:00.

Four minutes, switch at two. Keep it casual.

What just happened

That was networking.

You showed someone a thing you made and talked about it. That’s the whole skill.

Let it land. Ask: who learned something about the other person’s class from their app?

The next few weeks

Build something you care about. Then talk about it.

That’s what this club is for.

The goal for the coming weeks: a project you’re passionate about, and the words to pitch it.

Before next Thursday

Finish your profile. Connect with three people from today.

Then save it as a PDF. That’s your resume, draft one.
